title: He did not fall in one night.
paragraphs: He did not fall in one night.

Solomon — the wisest king on earth — multiplied wives, and with them came divided worship, divided desire, divided obedience. First Kings 11 does not just expose lust. It exposes what happens when a man keeps collecting what God never approved.
Because he stopped bowing to it.

The tragedy is not merely that Solomon loved many women. The deeper wound is that “his wives turned away his heart after other gods” (1 Kings 11:4). The man who built the temple started building altars for compromise. That is how sin works. It rarely begins with a public collapse. It starts with private permissions.

This is not just Solomon’s story. This is ours. We keep adding what feeds the flesh, then act shocked when the heart grows cold toward God. More attention. More validation. More secret indulgence. More excuses. And every “more” whispers the same lie: you can keep your appetite and keep your devotion too.
A divided heart will always drag devotion to the ground.
And that’s where grace walks in.

Because where Solomon’s love scattered, Jesus’ love stays faithful. Where Solomon compromised, Christ obeyed perfectly. Where earthly kings break covenant, Jesus keeps covenant with sinners who repent. The answer to a wandering heart is not self-hatred. It is surrender. Real repentance. Real turning. Real healing at the feet of the King who still restores ruined people.
So hear me clearly: your compromises do not have to be your coronation story. In Christ, the cycle can break. The idols can fall. The heart can come home.
Repent while your heart still feels His voice.
“His wives turned away his heart.” — 1 Kings 11:3–4
